title: Text-First Feature Browser
takeaway: A second published interface that inverts the usual view: instead of picking a feature and seeing the texts it fires on, you pick a text and see every feature active anywhere in it, ranked, each with a machine-written label. Hovering a token re-ranks the list for that token; hovering a feature paints its activation back onto every token. This is tooling for auditing the decomposition, not evidence for any claim.
walkthrough:
Three screenshots of one browser tool, in the three states it moves through as you move the mouse. This is the [[data-oriented-interface]], and it inverts the main [[feature-exploration-interface]], which starts from a single feature and shows the texts it fires on. Here you start from a text.

### The resting state

The left panel fixes one dataset example — the closing stanza of Keats's "Ode on a Grecian Urn", preceded by the `<EOT>` token that opens the context. Every token carries an orange shade.

Below the text sits a table of every [[feature]] the [[sparse-autoencoder]] finds active somewhere in this stanza: `Index`, `Act`, `% of Max`, `Autointerpreted Label`.

The label column is written by a language model from examples of when the unit fires; that pipeline is [[automated-interpretability]]. The prompt frames the unit as a neuron, which is why every label opens "This neuron…" even though these rows are learned features.

### Reading the two activation columns

Feature #447 shows $1.281$ and $19.03\%$. Dividing, $1.281 / 0.1903 \approx 6.73$. In the middle panel the same feature shows $3.026$ and $44.95\%$, and $3.026 / 0.4495 \approx 6.73$ again.

So `% of Max` normalises each [[feature-activation]] by that feature's own largest activation over the dataset — the same normalisation behind the paper's [[activation-interval]]s. The percentages are per-feature, so they are not comparable across rows as raw strengths.

### The two hovers

The middle panel hovers the token `generation`. The list re-sorts by activation at that token, and the top row turns deep orange: #447 at $3.026$, then #174, #227, #496. Feature #448, second in the whole-text list, has dropped out of the top four. One archaic-language feature dominates that token; the rest are weak.

The right panel hovers row #504, labelled as firing on "a comma followed by the word 'and'". Its activation is painted across the stanza. Commas light up, including commas that are not followed by "and", so the written label looks approximate rather than exact.

That is the use of the tool. You can check a label against a text token by token, in either direction. No number in the figure is a result.

terms.term: "For a selection of texts, we show all the active features." (left panel heading)
terms.definition: The resting state of the interface: a fixed piece of text with a table below it listing every feature that fires anywhere in that text. The paper offers this view for a set of chosen example texts, not for arbitrary input.

terms.term: "Hovering over a token will reveal the top activating features for that token" (middle panel heading)
terms.definition: The first interaction: pointing at one token re-sorts the table so the features are ranked by how strongly they fire on that token specifically, rather than on the text as a whole.

terms.term: "Hovering over a feature will show its activation on each of the tokens" (right panel heading)
terms.definition: The second interaction: pointing at one table row shades every token in the text by that single feature's activation there, so a written label can be checked against the text.

The column giving each active unit's number inside the dictionary, shown as a blue link (#447, #448, …) that presumably opens that unit's own page in the main feature interface. All six visible indices fall below 512; the figure does not name which dictionary learning run is on screen.

The column giving the activation value — the scalar the autoencoder's ReLU hidden unit takes. In the resting and feature-hover states it is a per-text number; when a token is hovered it becomes that feature's activation on that token.

The column giving the activation as a percentage of that feature's own maximum activation over the dataset. It rescales each feature onto its personal 0–100% range, so it says how strongly a feature is firing relative to itself, not relative to other rows.
The column holding a natural-language description of the unit, written by a language model from examples of tokens where the unit fires. It is a guess about the unit, not a verified property of it.

terms.term: "This neuron …" (the opening words of every label)
terms.definition: The autointerpretability prompt describes whatever unit it is shown as a neuron, so the generated labels say "neuron" even when the row is a learned feature rather than an MLP neuron. The paper elsewhere keeps the two strictly apart in notation.

The strongest unit on this text, labelled as firing on elevated, formal or old-fashioned language — "thou", "hast", "thy", "verily", archaic verb forms like "knowest", and titles like "lord" and "sir". It tops both the whole-text list and the list for the hovered token.

Labelled as attending to formal or archaic religious language: worshipping, professing belief, preaching, praying, invoking God. Second on the whole-text list, but absent from the top four for the token "generation".

Labelled as attending to medical and biomedical terminology — conditions, treatments, procedures, diagnoses, anatomy. Its presence on a Keats stanza is a reminder that a weakly firing unit's label need not describe why it fired here.
Labelled as firing when there is a comma followed by the word "and". This is the row hovered in the right panel, and its painted activation lands on commas generally, not only on commas before "and".
Labelled as firing on the term "here" and on words about stating facts or sharing information. It appears only in the token-hover list, ranked second for the token "generation".
Labelled as firing on present participle verb forms (-ing) and similar-sounding endings such as -ington and -ation. It ranks fourth for the token "generation", whose ending matches that description.
The end-of-text token that begins the context window, marking the start of a fresh document. It is heavily shaded in the first two panels and unshaded under feature #504.

The background colour on each token in the text pane, darker for more activation. In the resting state it summarises the total feature activity on a token; under a feature hover it shows that one feature's activation.
The highlight on #447 in the middle panel, marking the top-ranked feature for the hovered token. The remaining rows keep the pale background.
The small popup naming the token currently under the cursor, so it is unambiguous which token the re-ranked list belongs to. Tokenization means the displayed unit need not be a whole word.
The end-of-line marker shown at the close of each verse line, making newline tokens visible as tokens rather than as invisible whitespace.
The dataset example under inspection: the final stanza of Keats's "Ode on a Grecian Urn". It is a piece of text chosen for display, not a result about poetry.

A partly visible row below #504 ("This neuron seems to fire for examples of words or…") showing that the table scrolls. The figure therefore does not reveal how many features are active on the text in total.

numbers.meaning: Panels in the figure — one interface in three states: resting, token hovered, feature hovered.
Feature #447's whole-text activation and the same value as a share of its dataset maximum. The two together imply a maximum of about $1.281/0.1903 \approx 6.73$.
Feature #448's whole-text activation. Implied maximum $0.451/0.076 \approx 5.93$, so this feature is firing at well under a tenth of its usual peak.
Feature #227's whole-text activation. Implied maximum $0.291/0.0333 \approx 8.74$ — a weak firing of a feature whose label is about biomedical text.
Feature #504's whole-text activation, unchanged between the left and right panels because hovering a row paints the text without re-computing the row. Implied maximum $0.211/0.0242 \approx 8.72$.

The same feature evaluated at one token instead of the whole text. It is more than twice the resting value, and the ratio again gives $\approx 6.73$, confirming that % of Max divides by a fixed per-feature constant.
Second-ranked feature for that token. Implied maximum $0.825/0.1375 = 6.00$.
Third-ranked feature for that token, up from 0.291 in the whole-text list. Implied maximum $\approx 8.74$, matching its resting-state ratio.
Fourth-ranked feature for that token; the -ation ending of "generation" matches its label. Implied maximum $0.340/0.052 \approx 6.54$.

Not printed in the figure, but recoverable by dividing Act by % of Max. They differ from feature to feature, which is why the percentage column is needed at all: a raw activation of 0.5 means something different for each row.
Every feature active on this stanza is firing far below its own peak. The paper notes elsewhere that most real activations are small, and that low activations are the harder ones to interpret.
Identifiers within the dictionary, not quantities — the numbering carries no ordering or meaning. Every visible index is below 512, which the figure leaves unexplained.
The table is cut off by the screenshot rather than exhausted; a fifth row is partly readable in the left and right panels, so the true count of active features on this text is not shown.
